description: Somos un equipo versátil que convierte la diversidad de perfiles en su mayor fortaleza. Combinamos programación, diseño, ciencia de datos y comunicación para adaptarnos a cualquier reto que el espacio nos plantee. No nos limitamos a un solo rol: cada integrante aprende, aporta y cambia de enfoque según lo necesite el proyecto. Usamos los datos abiertos de la NASA para crear soluciones flexibles, creativas y con impacto real aquí en la Tierra.
summary: SowOrbit is a free, open-source web tool that helps farmers in Peru's Andean highlands choose crop rotations using NASA data. A farmer marks their plot anywhere in the sierra above 2,500 m, says what matters most to them (water, soil, erosion, fodder or climate), and gets three rotations compared side by side, each with a month-by-month frost and drought risk calendar, a confidence level and the source behind every number. The engine runs on NASA POWER climate records (1991-2024), corrected with SENAMHI's PISCO data because POWER underestimates highland frost, while NASA SRTM 30 m terrain adds slope around 22 pilot sites to flag erosion risk and MODIS NDVI shows when nearby fields and pastures are greenest. Everything runs in the browser with no server or account, and results can be downloaded as PDF reports to discuss with a local extension agent. This matters because highland families plant almost blind to shifting frost and rainfall patterns, and a single bad frost can wipe out a potato harvest. SowOrbit turns decades of NASA climate data into a simple, honest recommendation that shows what it knows and what it doesn't. It already covers the whole Peruvian sierra, and the same approach can extend to other mountain regions with local climate data.
details:
What it does:

SowOrbit is a free web tool that helps smallholder farmers in Peru's Andean highlands decide which crop rotation to plant, using NASA climate and terrain data. The farmer marks their plot on a satellite map (or searches for their town), rates five priorities from 0 to 5 (saving water, improving soil, reducing erosion, producing fodder for livestock, and coping with the local climate) and in seconds gets three 4-year rotations compared side by side. Rotation A is the traditional Cajamarca sequence (potato, maize, wheat, fallow). Rotation B adds faba bean to fix nitrogen and ends with forage oat for dairy cattle. Rotation C uses tarwi and vetch, which tolerate drought, fix nitrogen and keep the soil covered.

How it works:

For the chosen point, the app pulls daily and monthly NASA POWER data for 1991-2024 (T2M, T2M_MIN, PRECTOTCORR) and builds a 12-month climate profile with mean temperature, rainfall, rainfall variability and the share of years with at least one frost day. Because POWER's coarse grid smooths out the mountains and underestimates highland frost, we correct it with SENAMHI's PISCO gridded observations, precomputed for 22 pilot sites and calculated live in the browser for any other point above 2,500 m. Slope comes from NASA SRTM 30 m (processed through AppEEARS) around the pilots and from Copernicus DEM elsewhere. A transparent rule-based engine then scores each crop month by month, penalizing frost risk weighted by the crop's cold sensitivity, water deficit weighted by its drought tolerance, and temperatures outside its optimal range. Each rotation gets a 0-100 score on the five criteria, which are combined with the farmer's own weights. Around four pilots, MODIS NDVI (2014-2024), filtered to cropland and grassland with MODIS land cover, tells the farmer when local fields are greenest. It is shown as context and does not change the score.

What the farmer sees:

A card for each rotation with a plain-language explanation, year-by-year photos of the crops, a frost and drought risk calendar, a radar chart comparing the three options, and a confidence level shown by color and text. Frost risk is written as natural frequencies ("1 in 3 years") instead of percentages. Every result can be exported as a PDF report that lists the data sources, the agronomic evidence (FAO, INIA Peru, INIA Chile), the known limits and questions to ask the local extension agent.

Benefits and intended impact:

Highland families make planting decisions with little access to climate information, while frost and irregular rains increasingly destroy harvests. SowOrbit turns three decades of NASA data into a choice they can understand and discuss, and nudges them toward rotations with legumes and ground cover that rebuild soil and reduce erosion. It already covers the whole Peruvian sierra, needs no account or installation, and is MIT licensed so agencies, NGOs or other teams can adapt it to other mountain regions.

Tools and technologies:

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with no backend, hosted on GitHub Pages. Leaflet for the map, Chart.js for the charts, jsPDF for the exports. Python scripts (with numpy and rasterio for rasters) to process NASA POWER, AppEEARS (SRTM, MODIS NDVI and land cover) and PISCO data into static JSON, plus Node scripts to build the selectable area and lake mask. Over 80 automated tests cover the scoring engine, data loading, NDVI and terrain calculations. Imagery comes from Esri, NASA GIBS and OpenStreetMap.

What makes it creative:

Instead of a black-box answer, it compares options and explains why each one wins or loses. It combines a global NASA dataset with a national one to fix a known weakness of satellite climate data in the mountains. And it is honest about uncertainty, showing what the tool knows and what it doesn't.

Factors we considered:

Our users may have basic phones, weak connections and limited technical reading, so the app is static, light, written in plain language, and never relies on color alone. The interface is currently in English for global judging. It was first built in Spanish, and a Spanish and Quechua version for farmers is our next step. Crop parameters are literature estimates and are labeled as such. The climate describes past years, not a forecast. Our first MODIS request sampled city centers and measured roofs instead of fields, so we requested a new grid and kept only cropland and grassland pixels. SMAP soil moisture had too many gaps and low-quality retrievals in the mountains, so we left it out, and for that reason confidence never reaches "High". The tool supports the local agronomist, it does not replace them.

SI use:

We used AI coding assistants to speed up development. Claude Code (by Anthropic) helped write and review parts of the code and tests and draft this project description. OpenAI Codex assisted with the English translation of the interface and documentation. The team chose the data sources, the rotations and the scoring rules, and verified the results. No images, video or audio were generated with SI, and no NASA branding was created or modified with SI. The crop photos are real photos from Wikimedia Commons, credited in the app.
